title: Tissue stiffening induces histone serotonylation and primes migratory cell states in vivo - Nature Cell Biology
byline: Saraiva; Joana E; Wei; Xiaoran; Espina; Jaime A; Ribeiro; Miguel; Ramos; Ana Patricia; Korovesi; Artemis G; Maze; Ian; Barriga; Elias H
html:
Abstract

Collective cell migration (CCM) is pivotal in several biological contexts, and post-translational modifications of histones have been implicated in the onset of this process. Here we provide evidence for the involvement of a recently discovered chromatin marker, termed histone serotonylation, in the CCM of cranial neural crest (NC) cells—an embryonic multipotent stem cell population. Our in vivo data revealed that histone serotonylation occurs in NC cells just before they start migrating and that its occurrence supports their CCM. Notably, we found that stiffening of the NC cells’ migratory substrate, the mesoderm, induces histone serotonylation by promoting the nuclear translocation of transglutaminase 2 (Tgm2), an enzyme that catalyses the addition of serotonin to histones. Moreover, mechanical and molecular perturbations establish that shuttling of Tgm2 into the nucleus and concomitant increases in histone serotonylation are essential to trigger CCM in vivo. Furthermore, a combination of sequencing analyses is consistent with the idea that histone serotonylation is associated with a chromatin landscape that supports the switch from non-migratory to migratory cell states.

Main

A number of chromatin post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as histone methylation and acetylation, are involved in the initiation of CCM in neural crest cells and other cell types1,2,3. One of the main functions of PTMs is to fine-tune the chromatin landscape to allow for appropriate patterns of gene expression that control cell fate decisions and plasticity2,3. One such mark, histone H3 lysine (K) 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), is required for neural crest CCM and plays critical roles in the reinforcement of permissive gene expression1,2,3. Emerging evidence suggests that the maintenance of H3K4me3 is influenced by adjacent H3 glutamine (Q) 5 serotonylation, a recently discovered chromatin PTM that is written, erased and exchanged by the transglutaminase 2 (Tgm2) enzyme4. Functionally, serotonylation of histone H3 at Q5 facilitates the binding of H3K4me3 reader proteins (for example, the TFIID complex) and inhibits interactions with KDM5 and LSD1 demethylases, which remove H3K4 methylation4,5. Given the importance of H3K4me3 and serotonin in the development of neural crest cells6,7, we sought to explore whether histone serotonylation may operate during the collective migration of neural crest cells.

Results

Histone serotonylation supports neural crest collective cell migration

We first analysed the occurrence of histone serotonylation in non-migratory, pre-migratory and migratory neural crest cells in vivo (Fig. 1a,b) via immunofluorescence and western blot analyses. Our temporal analyses revealed that histone serotonylation levels display a robust increase when neural crest cells transition from non-migratory to pre-migratory stages, an increase that is sustained during migration (Fig. 1b–e). Next, we investigated whether this increase in histone serotonylation plays a role in the neural crest CCM. For this purpose, we used a previously described form of histone H3, which, owing to the replacement of H3Q5 with an alanine (A; H3Q5A), prevents histone serotonylation4 (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Microinjection of the wild-type (WT) form of H3 did not affect histone serotonylation, but H3Q5A microinjection reduced neural crest histone serotonylation both in vivo (Fig. 1f,g) and ex vivo (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). This finding confirms the effectiveness of this construct in affecting histone serotonylation as well as the specificity of the antibody for detecting this marker in both western blot (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f) and immunofluorescence. Thus, we next assessed the impact of H3Q5A on neural crest CCM via in situ hybridization against the migratory neural crest marker sox8. Stereotypical migratory streams were evident in embryos injected with a WT version of histone H3, but in H3Q5A-treated animals, the signal of sox8 accumulated in the dorsal part of the embryo (Fig. 1h–j), where the neural crest was originally located before the CCM. Similarly, ex vivo cell migration assays revealed that H3Q5A-treated neural crest cells failed to spread and migrate when compared with WT H3-injected neural crest cells (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i and Supplementary Video 1), indicating a specific requirement of histone serotonylation for the CCM in the neural crest. Control experiments confirmed the specificity of our results, as we observed that H3Q5A injection did not alter the occurrence of other chromatin marks that are relevant for neural crest specification1,7 (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f) or the expression of neural crest progenitor markers (Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). Together, these observations indicate that while not being required for neural crest specification, the occurrence of histone serotonylation is involved in the onset of CCM in vivo.

Mesoderm stiffening allows histone serotonylation

Given its recent discovery, the environmental or epigenetic factors that modulate the occurrence of histone serotonylation remain largely unknown. In Xenopus, the onset of neural crest CCM is mechanically controlled by stiffening the tissue that they use as a migratory substrate, the mesoderm8. Considering that mechanical stimuli also affect other chromatin modifications in other systems9, we next tested the involvement of mesoderm stiffening in histone serotonylation. For this purpose, we generated embryos with softened mesoderm by using a previously validated tool relying on targeted injections of an active form of myosin phosphatase-1 (CA-MYPT)8 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b and Fig. 2a). Notably, mesoderm softening resulted in a non-autonomous reduction in histone serotonylation in the neural crest (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 3c–e). Similarly, we assessed the role of mechanosensing in histone serotonylation by targeting vinculin, a key component of the machinery used by the neural crest to detect mesoderm stiffening8. Using a validated vinculin-Cter mutant that disrupts the onset of CCM8, we found that vinculin inhibition reduced histone serotonylation in vivo (Fig. 2b,c). Western blot analyses of isolated neural crests further confirmed these observations (Fig. 2d,e). To more directly corroborate the non-autonomous role of substrate mechanics in the regulation of histone serotonylation, we used an ex vivo assay that relies on the use of fibronectin-coated hydrogels with stiffness values similar to those found in the mesoderm at non-migratory (soft) and early migratory (stiff) stages8 (Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). In this scenario, we found that WT neural crest clusters plated on stiff hydrogels presented increased levels of histone serotonylation, but exposure to more compliant surfaces was sufficient to reduce the occurrence of this marker (Fig. 2f,g) to levels equivalent to those reported in non-migratory neural crests (Fig. 1b–e). Vinculin inhibition also prevented histone serotonylation in cells plated on stiff substrates (Fig. 2f,g), confirming the requirement for mechanosensing. Intriguingly, mechanical perturbations did not alter the cooccurring mark H3K4me3 (Extended Data Fig. 4a–e), implying that substrate mechanics specifically regulate histone serotonylation. Taken together, these data indicate that the mechanical properties of the mesoderm modulate the occurrence of histone serotonylation at the onset of neural crest CCM.

Histone serotonylation and substrate stiffening are associated with a permissive chromatin landscape

We next investigated whether histone serotonylation is associated with chromatin landscapes in the context of substrate mechanics. To this end, we integrated WT migratory ATAC-seq10, H3K4me3Q5ser ChIP−seq11 and RNA-seq datasets obtained from dissected migratory neural crest cells (Fig. 3a). We first mapped chromatin accessibility using ATAC-seq10 (Extended Data Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 1) and assessed the enrichment of histone serotonylation at accessible loci by ChIP−seq11 against H3K4me3Q5ser. This analysis revealed enrichment at proximal regulatory elements of numerous loci (Extended Data Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 2), consistent with the known permissive roles of this mark4,5. Intersection with RNA-seq data (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 3) identified a candidate set of 3,305 loci that are accessible, enriched in histone serotonylation and transcribed in WT migratory neural crest cells, and curated Gene Ontology (GO) term analysis supported an enrichment for migration-related processes (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Fig. 5c,d and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). We next asked which components of this WT migratory landscape were sensitive to perturbations that interfere with histone serotonylation or mechanical signalling (Fig. 3c). Candidates displaying a loss of chromatin accessibility in both H3Q5A and CA-MYPT ATAC-seq datasets were selected, and directional concordance in RNA-seq was used to link accessibility changes to transcriptional outputs (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Tables 6–9). This filtering yielded 378 candidates whose proximal regulatory elements are enriched in histone serotonylation and sensitive to substrate mechanics (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 10; details in Methods). As shown by GO term enrichment analysis of the full candidate set, the list includes candidates associated with morphogenesis, development, cell surface signalling, cell projections and cytoskeleton organization, cell junctions and cell movement, and includes candidates such as tubb6.S12, tcf4.L13, fdx1.L14, epha4.S15, exoc6b.L16, foxd1.L17, abhd17b.S18, wnt9a.S19, rasa3.S20 and ephb1.S21, among several others (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 11). Motif analysis of the accessible regulatory regions linked to the 378 candidates identified putative binding sites for transcription-factor families implicated in neural crest development, cell migration and mechanotransduction, among other families (Supplementary Table 12). Motif occurrences were assigned to candidate genes through their linked accessible regions, providing predicted motif annotations for all 378 candidates (Fig. 3h, Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 13). Note that these predicted binding sites still require experimental validations. Altogether, these analyses are consistent with histone serotonylation being associated with a permissive chromatin landscape that may support the onset of neural crest migration in response to substrate mechanics.
